extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, constitutional design, and public law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating normative principles and practical standards for designing and judging forms of government (separation of powers, balance of property, militia, representation, judicial safeguards, etc.). Useful for constitutional theorists, legislators, and historians of political thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of the three powers
rubrics_metrics.description: That of enacting laws, that of executing the public resolutions, and that of judging the crimes or differences of individuals should not be united in the same person or body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same man or body exercises all three powers, there will be an end of liberty and a tendency toward despotism; examples given include the Sultan in Turkey and certain Italian republics where the union of powers produced oppression (e.g., state inquisitors at Venice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judicial power concentrated in permanent bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary power ought not to be given to a standing senate; it should be exercised by persons taken from the body of the people at certain times and pursuant to a form and manner prescribed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary, law-prescribed tribunals that last only as long as necessity requires make the power of judging less visible and less threatening to citizens; this prevents judges from being constantly present and feared as magistrates rather than offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments must conform to the exact letter of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Though tribunals ought not to be fixed, the judgments ought to be always conformable to the exact letter of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If judgments were based on the private opinion of judges, people would not know exactly the obligations imposed by society; predictability of law is necessary for liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of accused to influence choice of judges
rubrics_metrics.description: In accusations of a deep or criminal nature, the person accused should have the privilege of choosing, in some measure, his judges, or at least a right to except against so many that the remaining part may be deemed his own choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving the accused some control over the composition of judges helps ensure fairness in grave criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges should be peers of the accused
rubrics_metrics.description: The judges ought likewise to be in the same station as the accused, or, in other words, his peers, so that he may not imagine he is fallen into the hands of persons inclined to treat him with rigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having peers adjudicate preserves perceived fairness and reduces the accused's fear of biased harshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature must not give indefinite imprisonment power to executive
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legislative leaves the executive power in possession of a right to imprison those subjects who can give security for their good behaviour, there is an end of liberty, unless they are taken up to answer without delay for a capital crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent executive power to detain persons with only nominal security undermines liberty; short, limited exceptional detention (authorised for a brief time in emergencies) may be permissible to preserve the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited emergency detention as exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legislature thinks itself in danger from secret conspiracy or correspondence with a foreign enemy, it might authorize the executive, for a short and limited time, to imprison suspected persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such detention must be strictly time-limited and exceptional; this is the only reasonable substitute to tyrannical magistracy in certain historic cases (e.g., Ephori, state inquisitors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power ideally resides in the whole body of the people (via representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: As, in a free state, every man who is supposed a free agent ought to be his own governor; so the legislative power should reside in the whole body of the people. Because this is impossible in large states, people should execute it by their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation is a practical necessity in large polities — representatives act on behalf of local inhabitants who best understand local wants and capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives should be chosen locally by inhabitants
rubrics_metrics.description: The members therefore of the legislature should not be chosen from the general body of the nation; but it is proper that in every considerable place a representative should be elected by the inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local election ensures representatives are familiar with local needs and neighbors' capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative advantage: capacity to discuss affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The great advantage of representatives is their being capable of discussing affairs; for this the people collectively are extremely unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegated deliberation avoids chaos and enables reasoned policy-making that a mass assembly could not achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives should not wait for specific instruction on every matter
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that representatives who have received a general instruction from their electors should wait to be particularly instructed on every affair; doing so causes delays and gives each deputy power to control the assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates should act with general mandates to avoid paralysis and undue influence by individual deputies; excessive micro-instruction (as in some German diets) impedes urgent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple tribunals/ magistracies temper each other
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of magistrates sometimes softens the power of the magistracy; different tribunals are erected that temper each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But if different tribunals are composed of magistrates all belonging to the same body, they effectively constitute one power; institutional diversity matters only if membership is independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified power enables plunder and private ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole power is united in one body, they might plunder the state by their general determinations; and as they have likewise the judiciary power in their hands, every private citizen may be ruined by their particular decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation and checks are necessary to prevent concentration of legislative, executive, and judicial functions enabling arbitrary confiscation or ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public sword (militia) must be held by someone with resources — ties to property
rubrics_metrics.description: The public sword, without a hand to hold it, is but cold iron. The militia of a nation is either an army in the field or ready for the field; an army must be fed and comes to depend on pastures (resources) — which ties the public sword to the balance of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whoever can maintain the military force (through property/resources) holds real power; distribution of property thus affects control of the militia and the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of property in land is foundation of forms of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of dominion in land (property) is the natural cause of empire: if one man be sole landlord of a territory he is absolute monarch; if the few be landlords it makes a mixed monarchy; if the whole people be landlords it is a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harrington's formulation: property distribution determines whether government tends to monarchy, aristocracy/oligarchy, or popular commonwealth; altering that balance by law or force transforms constitutional form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnatural imposition of force distorts legitimate government
rubrics_metrics.description: If force be interposed in any of the three cases, it must either frame the government to the foundation or the foundation to the government; otherwise it is not natural but violent and becomes tyranny, oligarchy, or anarchy depending on who holds power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy depends on concordance between social foundations (property) and governmental form; violent mismatch yields instability and illegitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of wealth threatens political stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Immoderate wealth, where one man or two have greater possessions than equality or the frame of the commonwealth will bear, is an occasion of sedition and tends toward monarchy; better to prevent growth early than to remedy it later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive laws addressing accumulation (e.g., agrarian laws) are recommended to avoid later violent corrections (debt rejection, expropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agrarian/founding laws fixing balance of land stabilize regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws fixing the balance in lands (called Agrarian laws) make the constitution immoveable; examples include Lycurgus's division and ancient Israel's lot division of Canaan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal measures that prevent unequal accumulation of land are presented as a durable means to preserve the intended balance of property and political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of government and their military resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: All government is of three kinds: a government of servants (absolute monarchy), a government of subjects (aristocratical monarchy), or a government of citizens (commonwealth). Government of servants is harder to conquer and easier to hold; government of subjects is easier to conquer and harder to hold; government of citizens is both hardest to conquer and hardest to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commonwealth of citizens, with broad militia training and attachment to liberty, provides strong defence but is difficult to sustain over time; these tradeoffs should inform constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative composition should reflect local knowledge and capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: The inhabitants of a particular town are much better acquainted with its wants and interests, and are better judges of the capacity of their neighbours than of that of the rest of their countrymen; therefore representatives should be elected locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local selection yields more informed representatives and aligns legislative action with local needs; central selection from a general pool is less effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks among political orders preserve liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniting advantages and properties of the best governments (kingly, aristocratical, democratical) so that each branch may be opposed and balanced by the others prevents any branch from swelling into its degenerate vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lycurgus' model: combining and balancing the powers (king/people/senate) restrains excesses and preserves liberty — e.g., consuls restrained by fear of people and senate, senate by consuls and people, etc.
